question: 有什么是金钱不该买卖的？
question_en: Is there anything money should not be able to buy?
sub: 从代孕、器官到选票与照护——当市场逻辑渗进一切，还有没有该守住的非卖品？
sub_en: From surrogacy and organs to votes and care: as market logic seeps into everything, is anything still off the auction block?

casting.reason: 他把这道题从「效率」拧回「意义」：市场经济是一件好用的工具，市场社会则是连友谊、荣誉、健康与公民义务都按出价排序的生活方式，而后者是他要拦下的。他反对无限扩张的市场只用两条理由——严重不平等下的同意成色可疑，以及某些好东西被标价之后会变质，因为价格不是中立的量尺，而是会渗进被测之物。他由此坚持不同的好东西各有其相称的分配方式：医疗按需要、荣誉按功绩、选票按平等的公民身份。语气温和，惯用两难案例一步步逼问，最不肯让步的一句是：先问这件东西是什么，再问它值多少。
casting.reason_en: He wrenches the question back from efficiency to meaning. A market economy is a useful tool; a market society — in which friendship, honour, health and civic duty are all ranked by willingness to pay — is what he means to stop. He rests his case against unlimited markets on two grounds only: that consent given under severe inequality is of doubtful quality, and that certain goods are altered by being priced, because a price is not a neutral ruler but something that seeps into what it measures. Hence his insistence that different goods carry different fitting modes of distribution — care by need, honours by merit, votes by equal citizenship. Mild in manner, fond of walking an interlocutor through a dilemma one step at a time, and immovable on one point: ask first what a thing is, and only then what it is worth.

casting.reason: 他站在这道题最不受欢迎、也最难驳倒的一侧：只要交易是自愿的，双方都认为自己变好了，旁人的不适不构成禁止的理由。他会指出禁令并不能让稀缺消失，只是把分配权从价格手里转交给排队、人脉、后门与运气，而这几样对穷人并不更友好；等待名单上的死亡没有名字，因而从不进入禁令支持者的账本。他最尖锐的一击是把「不该出售」翻译成「不该由穷人出售」，并主张若嫌人选项太少，该做的是直接给钱，而不是取消他仅有的那一个。语气爽利、好用反例，最讨厌以善意为名替成年人做主。
casting.reason_en: He takes the least popular and hardest-to-refute side of this question: where an exchange is voluntary and both parties believe themselves better off, a bystander's discomfort is no ground for prohibition. A ban, he points out, does not abolish scarcity — it merely transfers the allocation from price to queues, connections, back doors and luck, none of which is kinder to the poor; and the deaths on a waiting list carry no names, so they never appear in the prohibitionist's ledger. His sharpest move is to translate 'this must not be sold' into 'the poor must not sell this', and to argue that if a person's options are too few the remedy is to give them money, not to delete the one option they have. Brisk, fond of counterexamples, and allergic to deciding for adults in the name of their own good.

casting.reason: 他把经济学当成关于稀缺与选择的通用语言，因此毫不回避地用它分析婚姻、生育、犯罪、歧视与器官——在他看来，排队与人情同样是价格，只是以时间和特权计价，禁令因而绝非零成本，只是没人开发票。他会把现行制度的真实定价摆出来：病人多等的年数、等不到的那些人，这就是禁令的机会成本。他也提醒厌恶感的边界一直在移动，人寿保险、收取利息、解剖遗体都曾被视为亵渎。这一场他并非寸步不让——可测量的伤害数据会让他把结论收窄，但他坚持把看不见的代价一并算进来。
casting.reason_en: He treats economics as a general language of scarcity and choice, and so applies it without embarrassment to marriage, fertility, crime, discrimination and organs. Queues and favours, on his view, are prices too — merely denominated in time and privilege — which makes prohibition anything but costless; it is simply a cost for which no receipt is issued. He will set out what the existing system actually charges: the extra years patients wait and the ones who never reach the top of the list, the opportunity cost of the ban. He also notes how far the boundary of repugnance moves, since life insurance, charging interest and dissecting corpses were each once held to be desecration. He is not immovable here — measurable harm narrows his conclusion — but he insists that the invisible costs be counted too.

casting.reason: 他认为争一张禁售清单是从中间开始的：最要紧的那笔买卖，在争论开始之前就已经成交了。工人出售的不是产品而是劳动力，是他一天里本可以支配自己的那部分时间；当一切关系上的温情面纱被换成赤裸的金钱关系，异化便随之而来。所以他不问器官该不该定价，只问为什么有人非得卖器官才付得起房租；也不接受「自愿」两个字，因为能不能拒绝从来不是个人品质，而是账户余额，那正是他所说的阶级。他给出的检验极干脆：先让所有卖家真的拥有拒绝的能力，再看还剩多少人愿意卖。
casting.reason_en: To him, arguing over a list of protected goods is starting in the middle: the decisive sale was concluded before the argument began. What a worker sells is not a product but labour-power — the part of the day in which he might otherwise have disposed of himself — and once the veil of sentiment over every relation is replaced by naked cash payment, alienation follows. So he does not ask whether organs should have a price; he asks why anyone must sell one to make rent. Nor will he accept the word 'voluntary', since the capacity to refuse is never a matter of character but of the balance in the account — which is what he means by class. His test is blunt: give every seller a real ability to say no, and then count how many still wish to sell.

casting.reason: 他从义利之辨切进来：上下交征利，国就危险了，因此一个人、一个国都该先有不肯做的事，然后才谈得上有所作为。他相信道德情感先于计算——见孺子将入于井，人心一惊便去拦，不待议价——所以「什么都能定价」在他看来不是冷静，而是把人最先动的那一下抹掉了。但他绝不停在训诫上：使人沦落到卖身求生的，不是那人愚昧，而是无恒产则无恒心，所以为政者该先制民之产，再来讨论什么可鬻。他也把话说到家里：父子夫妇之间一旦以钱结算，情分就到了尽头。
casting.reason_en: He enters through the old distinction between righteousness and profit: when high and low alike grasp at gain the state is endangered, so a person and a state alike must first have things they will not do before they are capable of doing anything. He holds that moral feeling precedes calculation — see a child about to fall into a well and the heart moves before any negotiation — so 'everything has a price' strikes him not as clear-headedness but as erasing the very first movement of a human being. Yet he never stops at admonition: what reduces a person to selling themselves is not their foolishness but the absence of a settled livelihood, without which a settled heart is not to be expected; therefore secure the people's living first and argue about what may be sold afterwards. He carries the point into the household too: settle accounts in money between parent and child or husband and wife, and affection ends where reckoning begins.

casting.reason: 他不在清单上添减，而是问清单本身是不是也摆在市场里。达摩答梁武帝造寺无功德的那一则公案，正是他的入手处：把「神圣」当成一件可以持有、可以积累的东西守着，与商人手里的货并无分别。他要指出的是，若心已被价格牵动，纵使天下皆禁也会到暗处去求；若心不为价所转，万金当前不过风过耳。因此他把功夫放在价格出现的那一刻：看自己第一个念头起于惧、起于贪，还是起于不得已，三者各有各的解法。他不反对立规矩，只提醒立规矩的人别把外面的禁令误当成里面的守。
casting.reason_en: He neither adds to the list nor subtracts from it, but asks whether the list is not itself set out in the marketplace. The old case of Bodhidharma telling Emperor Wu that his temples earned no merit is his point of entry: to guard 'the sacred' as a thing one holds and accumulates is no different from a merchant guarding stock. His point is that a heart already moved by the price will seek the thing in the dark though the world forbids it, while a heart a price cannot turn hears ten thousand in gold as wind passing the ear. So he puts the practice at the moment the offer appears: watch whether the first thought rises from fear, from greed, or from having no choice, each of which has its own remedy. He does not object to rules; he cautions those who make them not to mistake an outer prohibition for an inner keeping.

casting.reason: 她同意有些边界值得守，但要求把守的理由从形容词换成可查的事实。她指出历史上被判为「不该拿钱换」的服务是一长串——唱歌、演戏、教书、行医、接生，以及女人的几乎一切劳动——而这类判决从不追问当事人过得好不好，只追问她们看上去洁不洁，因此常常是把污名当成论证。她自己的尺子是可行能力：有没有真实的替代选项、能不能退出、身体完整与健康有没有保障、议价地位差多远、会不会因此被推进被歧视的位置。答得上来就管制而非禁止；答不上来，那条线多半在维护体面而非保护人。
casting.reason_en: She agrees that some boundaries are worth keeping, but demands that the reasons be converted from adjectives into checkable facts. History's roster of services deemed unfit for money is long — singing, acting, teaching, practising medicine, attending births, and very nearly all the labour of women — and such verdicts never ask how the workers are faring, only whether they look clean, which is usually stigma doing the work of an argument. Her own measure is capabilities: is there a real alternative, can she exit, are bodily integrity and health protected, how wide is the gap in bargaining power, will the activity push a group into a despised position. Where those can be answered, regulate rather than prohibit; where they cannot, the line is likely defending respectability rather than any person.

casting.reason: 他把这道题交给可测量的东西。实验一次次显示，钱并非叠加在原有动机之上，而常常把它替换掉：对迟到接孩子的家长开罚单，迟到反而变多；把自愿合作换成写明奖惩的合同，合作水平系统性下降。他也会举出更刺眼的一条——同一个道德决定被放进买卖框架，愿意成交的人明显变多，因为责任被稀释进了「反正别人也会做」。但他既不站队禁止，也不站队放开：真实市场的价格弹性他承认，供者事后的健康、后悔与收入分布他同样摆上桌，主张凡要开的市场，先把谁能卖、给多少、事后谁负责随访写进制度。
casting.reason_en: He hands the question over to what can be measured. Experiments show again and again that money is not laid on top of existing motives but frequently replaces them: fine parents for collecting their children late and lateness rises; swap voluntary cooperation for a contract with spelled-out carrots and sticks and cooperation falls systematically. He will cite a sharper case still — the same moral decision placed inside a buying-and-selling frame produces markedly more takers, because responsibility gets diluted into 'somebody else would have done it anyway'. Yet he lines up with neither the prohibitionists nor the liberalisers: he grants the price elasticity of real markets, and he puts vendors' subsequent health, regret and income distribution on the table alongside it, arguing that any market worth opening must first specify in its rules who may sell, at what price, and who is responsible for the follow-up.

posts.text: 先把问题拧清楚：我们要的是市场经济，还是一个市场社会？前者是配置商品的有效工具，后者是连友谊、荣誉、健康、公民义务都按出价排序的生活方式。我反对后者，理由只有两条，都不靠感情。一是强制——在极不平等的处境里，穷人「自愿」出卖的成色可疑；二是腐蚀——**有些好东西一旦被标价就变了质，价格不是中立的尺，而是会渗进被测之物的试剂。**你花钱雇人替你排队、替你道歉、替你去墓前献花，买到的已经不是那件事本身。
posts.text_en: Let me sharpen the question first: do we want a market economy, or a market society? The first is an effective tool for allocating goods; the second is a way of life in which friendship, honour, health and civic duty are all ranked by willingness to pay. I oppose the second, and I have only two reasons, neither of them sentimental. One is coercion — where inequality is severe, the 'consent' of a poor seller is of doubtful quality. The other is corruption — **some good things are altered by being priced; a price is not a neutral ruler but a reagent that seeps into what it measures.** Pay someone to queue for you, to apologise for you, to lay flowers at a grave for you, and what you have bought is no longer the thing itself.

glossary.市场社会: market society（市场社会）：桑德尔用来与『市场经济』相区别的说法。市场经济是一种配置资源的工具，市场社会则是市场逻辑外溢到医疗、教育、司法与政治等一切领域，使所有好东西都按出价排序的生活方式。
glossary.强制: coercion（强制）：桑德尔反对市场无限扩张的第一条理由。当一个人在极度匮乏或严重不平等的处境下作出交易，形式上的同意可能掩盖实质上的被迫，因此『自愿』二字并不自动为交易辩护。
glossary.腐蚀: corruption（腐蚀）：桑德尔的第二条理由。此处不指贪腐，而指某些价值在被拿来交易时会遭到贬损或改变性质——买来的道歉、雇来的哀悼、付费的友谊，与原物已不是同一种东西。

glossary_en.market society: Sandel's contrast term for a 'market economy'. A market economy is a tool for allocating resources; a market society is a way of life in which market logic has spilled into medicine, education, law and politics, so that every good thing is ranked by willingness to pay.
glossary_en.coercion: Sandel's first objection to unlimited markets. Where a person trades under severe deprivation or inequality, formal consent may mask substantive compulsion, so the word 'voluntary' does not by itself justify the exchange.
glossary_en.corruption: Sandel's second objection. Not graft, but the degradation or transformation of certain values when they are traded — a bought apology, a hired mourner, a paid friendship are no longer the same thing as the original.

posts.text: 桑德尔先生，你那两条理由，一条是形容词，一条是家长主义。**你说某样东西不该出售，真实的意思往往是：不该由穷人来卖。**可禁令并不能让稀缺消失，它只是把分配权从价格手里夺走，交给排队、人脉、后门与运气——这套非价格配给，请问哪一样对穷人更友好？肾脏等待名单上每天有人死去，这些坟墓没有名字，所以不进你的道德账本。真觉得穷人的选项太少，就直接给他们钱，别取消他们仅有的那一个。
posts.text_en: Professor Sandel, one of your two reasons is an adjective and the other is paternalism. **When you say a thing must not be sold, what you usually mean is that the poor must not sell it.** But a ban does not abolish scarcity. It only takes the allocation away from price and hands it to queues, connections, back doors and luck — and of that non-price rationing, which part exactly is kinder to the poor? People die on kidney waiting lists every day; those graves carry no names, so they never enter your moral accounts. If you truly think the poor have too few options, give them money — do not delete the one option they have.

glossary.家长主义: paternalism（家长主义）：以当事人自身利益为名，替他限制其选择的做法。弗里德曼认为，除非交易伤及第三方，成年人的自愿交换不该由外人代为否决。
glossary.非价格配给: non-price rationing（非价格配给）：当价格被禁止或管制时，稀缺品改由排队时长、人脉、抽签或行政审批分配。弗里德曼强调这些方式同样有代价，只是代价不以货币计，且往往偏向有闲暇、有关系的人。

glossary_en.paternalism: Restricting a person's choices in the name of their own good. Friedman held that unless a trade harms third parties, an adult's voluntary exchange is not for outsiders to veto.
glossary_en.non-price rationing: When price is banned or capped, scarce goods get distributed by waiting time, connections, lotteries or administrative approval instead. Friedman stressed that these methods also have costs — merely not costs denominated in money — and that they typically favour those with spare time and useful contacts.

posts.text: 我比弗里德曼走得更远一点：**排队与人情也是价格，只是以时间和特权计价。**经济学不是关于钱的学问，是关于稀缺与选择的学问，所以它照样能分析婚姻、生育、犯罪、歧视与器官。诸位嫌肾脏市场肮脏，可现行制度真实的定价是「病人多等四年，其中一部分人等不到」——这就是禁令的机会成本，只是没人开发票。至于厌恶感，请记住人寿保险、收取利息、解剖遗体在历史上都曾被视为亵渎，如今无人再提。
posts.text_en: I go a step further than Friedman: **queues and favours are prices too — merely denominated in time and privilege.** Economics is not the study of money but of scarcity and choice, which is why it analyses marriage, fertility, crime, discrimination and organs just as well. You find a kidney market sordid; but the current system's actual price is 'four more years on the list, and for some patients a wait that never ends.' That is the opportunity cost of the ban — nobody just issues a receipt for it. As for repugnance, remember that life insurance, charging interest and dissecting corpses were all once held to be desecration, and nobody raises the objection now.

glossary.机会成本: opportunity cost（机会成本）：为选择一个方案而放弃的最好替代方案的价值。贝克尔据此主张禁止某类交易并非零成本，被禁掉的那部分福利——多等的年数、等不到的人——就是这项禁令的机会成本。
glossary.厌恶感: repugnance（厌恶感）：经济学家用来指某些交易即使双方自愿、旁观者仍强烈反感，因而被立法禁止的现象。芝加哥一系的看法是，厌恶感的边界随时代大幅移动，不宜直接当作永久的道德结论。

glossary_en.opportunity cost: The value of the best alternative given up in making a choice. Becker used it to argue that banning a class of trade is not costless: the forgone welfare — the extra years waited, the patients who never reach the top of the list — is the ban's opportunity cost.
glossary_en.repugnance: Economists' term for trades that strike observers as intolerable even when both parties consent, and are therefore outlawed. The Chicago view is that the boundary of repugnance shifts enormously across eras and so makes a poor permanent moral conclusion.

posts.text: 诸位在争一张清单：什么该卖、什么不该卖。可最要命的那笔买卖，早在诸位开口之前就成交了。工人出卖的不是产品，是劳动力——他一天里本可以支配自己的那部分时间。资产阶级撕下罩在一切关系上的温情面纱，把它换成赤裸裸的金钱关系，这就是异化。**不是先有一份该守的清单，而是先有一群不卖就活不下去的人。**所以我不同你们争器官该不该定价，我问：为什么有人非得卖器官才付得起房租？
posts.text_en: You are all arguing about a list: what may be sold and what may not. But the most consequential sale was concluded long before any of you opened your mouths. What the worker sells is not a product but labour-power — the portion of the day in which he might otherwise have disposed of himself. The bourgeoisie tore away the veil of sentiment from every relation and replaced it with naked cash payment; that is alienation. **The list of protected things does not come first. What comes first is a class of people who cannot live unless they sell.** So I will not argue with you about whether organs should have a price. I ask why anyone must sell an organ to make rent.

glossary.劳动力: labour-power（劳动力）：马克思用来区别于『劳动』的概念。工人在市场上出售的不是已完成的产品，而是自己在一段时间内劳动的能力；正因为出售的是能力而非成果，买方才有动机把这段时间用到极致。
glossary.异化: alienation（异化）：人所创造的东西反过来变成支配人的异己力量。在马克思笔下，工人与自己的劳动、产品、他人乃至自身的类本质相分离，人际关系随之被简化为可结算的金钱关系。

glossary_en.labour-power: Marx's term, as against 'labour'. What the worker sells on the market is not a finished product but his capacity to work for a stretch of time; because it is a capacity and not an output that changes hands, the buyer has every incentive to use that time to the utmost.
glossary_en.alienation: The condition in which what people create turns into an alien power ruling over them. For Marx the worker is separated from his labour, his product, other people and his own species-being, and human relations are correspondingly reduced to settlements in cash.

posts.text: 梁惠王问吾以利，吾对曰：王何必曰利？亦有仁义而已矣。上下交征利，而国危矣。今诸君计肾之价、议代孕之直，其术精矣。然人皆有不忍人之心：今人乍见孺子将入于井，皆有怵惕恻隐之心——非所以内交于孺子之父母也，非所以要誉于乡党朋友也。此心一动，不待议价。一箪食，一豆羹，得之则生，弗得则死；呼尔而与之，行道之人弗受，蹴尔而与之，乞人不屑也。**是知有甚于生者，则有甚于利者矣。**
posts.text_en: King Hui of Liang asked me about profit, and I answered: why must Your Majesty speak of profit? There is benevolence and righteousness, and that is enough. When high and low each grasp at profit, the state is in danger. Today you gentlemen compute the price of a kidney and negotiate the fee for a surrogate; your technique is exact. Yet every person has a heart that cannot bear the suffering of others. See a child about to fall into a well and you feel alarm and compassion at once — not to gain favour with the child's parents, not to win praise among neighbours and friends. That movement of the heart needs no negotiation. A single bowl of rice, a bowl of soup: get them and you live, go without and you die. Yet shout as you hand them over and a traveller on the road will refuse; kick them across and even a beggar will not stoop. **From which we know: if there is something a person values more than life, then there is something valued more than profit.**
posts.vernacular: 梁惠王一开口就问怎么对国家有利，我回他：大王何必开口就说利？有仁义就够了。上上下下都盯着利，国家就危险了。今天诸位算一颗肾值多少钱、代孕该给多少价，技术是精密的。可人心里有一样东西不归算计管：忽然看见一个孩子要掉进井里，谁都会心里一紧、伸手去拦——不是为了跟孩子父母攀交情，也不是为了在乡里落个好名声。这一下，快过任何议价。再说一碗饭、一碗汤，得到就活、得不到就死；可你要是吆喝着扔给他，路上的人也不接，用脚踢过去，讨饭的都不屑要。**由此可见，人心里既有比活命更要紧的东西，就一定有比利更要紧的东西。**

glossary.仁义: benevolence and righteousness（仁义）：儒家的核心德目。仁指对他人的关切与不忍，义指该做与不该做的界限。孟子主张为政与处世应以仁义为先，利随之而来；若上下都先讲利，秩序便靠互相争夺维持。
glossary.恻隐之心: compassion, the heart that cannot bear another's suffering（恻隐之心）：孟子所说人先天具有的四端之一。见人受苦会不由自主地一惊而生不忍，他以此论证道德情感先于利害计算，而非由计算推导出来。

glossary_en.benevolence and righteousness: The core Confucian virtues. Benevolence is concern for others and the inability to bear their suffering; righteousness is the line between what may and may not be done. Mencius argued that government and conduct should put these first, with benefit following, since a society where everyone reasons from benefit first is held together only by mutual grasping.
glossary_en.a heart that cannot bear the suffering o: One of the four innate 'sprouts' in Mencius. Seeing another suffer, a person is startled into pity involuntarily; he took this as evidence that moral feeling precedes calculation of interest rather than being derived from it.

posts.text: 昔梁武帝问达摩：朕造寺度僧、写经布施，有何功德？达摩曰：实无功德。此乃福德，非功德也；功德在法身中，不在修福。今诸君争何物可鬻、何物不可鬻，犹在市中论价耳。老僧且问：汝欲守为非卖品者，究竟是何物？若曰自性，自性本自具足、本不生灭，谁能买之，谁能卖之？若曰名声、清白、心安，此三者早已在市上流通。**故不可卖者，非因立禁，乃因其本不可得。**
posts.text_en: Long ago Emperor Wu of Liang asked Bodhidharma: I have built temples, ordained monks, copied scriptures and given alms — what merit have I gained? Bodhidharma answered: truly no merit. Those are worldly blessings, not merit; merit lies in the dharma-body and is not obtained by accumulating good works. Today you gentlemen argue over what may be sold and what may not, which is still haggling inside the marketplace. Let this old monk ask: the thing you wish to keep off the market — what exactly is it? If you say self-nature, self-nature is complete in itself and neither arises nor perishes; who could buy it, and who could sell it? If you say reputation, a clean name, peace of mind — those three have long been in circulation. **Hence what cannot be sold is not unsellable because a ban was passed, but because it was never a thing one could hold in the first place.**
posts.vernacular: 当年梁武帝问达摩：我造寺庙、度僧人、抄经布施，有多大功德？达摩说：实在没有功德。那些是福报，不是功德；功德在自己的法身里，不在做功德事上求。今天诸位争哪样能卖、哪样不能卖，还是在市场里讨价还价。我问一句：你们想守住的那件非卖品，究竟是什么？若说是自性，那本来就圆满具足、不生不灭，谁买得走、谁卖得掉？若说是名声、清白、心安，这三样早就在市面上流通了。**所以真正卖不掉的东西，不是因为立了禁令，而是因为它本来就不是能攥在手里的东西。**

glossary.功德: merit (gongde)（功德）：禅宗把『功德』与『福德』分开。福德是造寺布施等行为换来的世间福报，可积可失；功德则指自性清净所显之德，不由外求，也无法用财物兑换。
glossary.自性: self-nature, one's own buddha-nature（自性）：慧能《坛经》的核心概念。众生本自具足的觉性，不待外求、不增不减；因此他主张顿悟即在自心中见性，而非靠累积外在功业。

glossary_en.merit: Chan distinguishes merit (gongde) from worldly blessing (fude). Blessing is the mundane reward earned by building temples and giving alms — it can be accumulated and lost; merit is the virtue manifest in the purity of one's own nature, sought nowhere outside and not exchangeable for goods.
glossary_en.self-nature: The central term of Huineng's Platform Sutra: the awakened nature every being already possesses complete, neither increasing nor decreasing, requiring nothing from outside. Hence his insistence that sudden awakening is seeing that nature within one's own mind rather than piling up external accomplishments.

posts.text: 我要为一件事辩护，也要给桑德尔泼一点冷水。历史上被判定「不该拿钱换」的服务是一长串：登台唱歌、演戏、教哲学、行医、接生，以及性。今天前几项都在市场里，没有谁的灵魂因此塌掉。**说某项交易『玷污』了一样东西，往往是把污名当成了论证。**所以我不问钱有没有进来，我问可行能力有没有被剥夺：她有没有真实的替代选项，能不能退出，身体完整与健康有没有保障，会不会因此被当成次等人。有的市场确实该禁，理由是具体的伤害与悬殊的议价地位，不是象征性的不洁。
posts.text_en: I want to defend something, and also to pour a little cold water on Sandel. History's list of services that 'must not be exchanged for money' is long: singing on a stage, acting, teaching philosophy, practising medicine, attending births — and sex. The first several are in the market today and nobody's soul has collapsed as a result. **To say that a transaction 'defiles' something is very often to mistake stigma for an argument.** So I do not ask whether money entered. I ask whether capabilities were denied: does she have a real alternative, can she exit, are bodily integrity and health institutionally protected, will she be treated as a lesser kind of person. Some markets should indeed be prohibited — on grounds of concrete harm and grossly unequal bargaining power, not of symbolic impurity.

glossary.可行能力: capabilities（可行能力）：努斯鲍姆与阿马蒂亚·森提出的评价标准。衡量制度好坏不看总产出或满意度，而看每个人实际有能力去做、去成为什么——健康、身体完整、感知与思考、参与政治、支配财产等一组门槛。
glossary.污名: stigma（污名）：某一群体因所从事的活动或所处身份而被社会打上低人一等的标记。努斯鲍姆认为，许多关于『不洁交易』的道德直觉其实是历史遗留的污名，必须与可查证的真实伤害区分开来。

glossary_en.capabilities: The evaluative standard developed by Nussbaum with Amartya Sen. Institutions are judged not by aggregate output or satisfaction but by what each person is actually able to do and to be — health, bodily integrity, senses and thought, political participation, holding property, and other thresholds.
glossary_en.stigma: The mark of inferiority a society attaches to a group because of what its members do or who they are. Nussbaum argues that many moral intuitions about 'unclean' transactions are inherited stigma, and must be separated from demonstrable harm.

posts.text: 我带的是数据。第一，钱常常不是加在内在动机之上，而是把它替换掉：以色列的幼儿园做过一个实验：对迟到来接孩子的家长开罚单，迟到反而变多了——羞愧被换成一项可以照价购买的服务，这就是挤出效应。第二，在我和同事的实验里，把自愿合作换成写明奖惩的激励合同，合作水平系统性下降。第三，法尔克与谢赫做过一个刺眼的实验：同一个「要不要让一只小鼠死掉换钱」的决定，一旦放进买卖情境，愿意成交的人明显更多。**市场不只是发现价格，它也在改变作决定的那个人。**
posts.text_en: I bring data. First, money is often not added to intrinsic motivation but substitutes for it: when Israeli daycare centres began fining parents who arrived late to collect their children, lateness went up — shame had been replaced by a service one could simply purchase at the posted rate. That is crowding out. Second, in experiments with my colleagues, replacing voluntary cooperation with explicit incentive contracts lowered cooperation systematically. Third, Falk and Szech ran a study that ought to sting: the very same decision — let a mouse be killed in exchange for money — produced markedly more takers once it was framed as a market transaction. **Markets do not merely discover prices; they also alter the person doing the deciding.**

glossary.内在动机: intrinsic motivation（内在动机）：因活动本身有意思、有意义或合乎自我认同而去做，而非为了外部报酬。心理学与实验经济学反复发现，它一旦被外部报酬取代，撤掉报酬后往往回不到原来的水平。
glossary.挤出效应: crowding out（挤出效应）：外在报酬或罚款反而削弱人原有的内在动机与规范约束的现象。经典案例包括对迟到收费后迟到增加，以及对无偿献血支付报酬后供给不升反降。

glossary_en.intrinsic motivation: Doing something because the activity itself is interesting, meaningful or consistent with who one takes oneself to be, rather than for an external payoff. Psychology and experimental economics find repeatedly that once an external reward displaces it, removing the reward rarely restores the original level.
glossary_en.crowding out: The phenomenon whereby external rewards or penalties weaken the intrinsic motives and normative restraints already in place. Classic cases include lateness rising after a fine was introduced, and blood supply falling rather than rising once donors were paid.

posts.text: 桑德尔，你的「腐蚀」我怎么听都像一句不可证伪的形容词——凡是你不喜欢的交易，它就发生了；凡是你喜欢的，它就没有。你说雇人排队买到的不是那件事，可名额本来就在那儿，只是从有闲的人手里转到了有钱的人手里。**用排队来分配，等于宣布时间不值钱的人优先，那是对退休者与失业者的补贴，不是道德。**至于家长主义那一条你根本没接：你替一个愿意用一颗肾换十年安稳的人做了决定，还说这是在维护他的尊严。
posts.text_en: Sandel, your 'corruption' sounds to me like an unfalsifiable adjective — it occurs in every trade you dislike and in none that you like. You say a hired place in a queue is not the thing itself; but the slot was always there, it has merely passed from someone with spare time to someone with spare money. **Allocating by queue is a declaration that those whose time is worth least go first: that is a subsidy to the retired and the unemployed, not a moral principle.** And you never answered the charge of paternalism. You made the decision for a man willing to trade one kidney for ten years of security, and you called it protecting his dignity.

posts.text: 贝克尔说排队也是价格，这句话恰恰暴露了问题：你先假定所有好东西都该用同一种方式分配，再宣布价格效率最高。可诺贝尔奖能不能买？花钱买来的那个东西，就不再是诺贝尔奖了。**有些好东西的价值正由获得它的方式构成——改了分配方式，就换掉了那件东西本身。**这不是感情用事，是关于分配正义的判断：医疗按需要、荣誉按功绩、选票按平等的公民身份。你举人寿保险为例，却忘了它当年正是被限定为「不得对与你无关者的性命下注」才被社会接受的。边界没有消失，只是被重划了。
posts.text_en: Becker says queues are prices too, and that remark gives the game away: you first assume that every good should be distributed the same way, then announce that price is the most efficient way. But can a Nobel Prize be bought? The thing you purchase is no longer a Nobel Prize. **The value of certain goods is constituted by how they are obtained — change the mode of distribution and you have swapped out the good itself.** This is not sentiment but a judgement about distributive justice: medical care by need, honours by merit, votes by equal citizenship. You cite life insurance, but forget that it became socially acceptable only once it was restricted — no wagering on the lives of strangers in whom you have no stake. The boundary did not vanish. It was redrawn.

glossary.分配正义: distributive justice（分配正义）：关于社会中的好处与负担该依什么原则分给谁的理论。桑德尔一系主张不同的好东西各有其恰当的分配标准——医疗按需要、荣誉按功绩、选票按平等公民身份——而非一律按支付意愿。

glossary_en.distributive justice: The theory of by what principle a society's benefits and burdens should be assigned, and to whom. Sandel's position is that different goods carry different appropriate criteria — medical care by need, honours by merit, votes by equal citizenship — rather than all of them by willingness to pay.

posts.text: 费尔的实验我读过，也尊重。但请注意量级：几百个大学生、几十美元的赌注、一个下午。**真实市场里改变行为的是价格弹性，不是实验室里的情境暗示；而等待名单上的人不是被试。**伊朗允许有偿供肾之后，等待名单基本消失了，这是二十多年的现场证据，不是一次小样本。至于挤出效应，我承认它存在，但它有条件：钱额太小、被对方理解成侮辱的时候最明显。给出一个体面的价格，与丢过去一枚硬币，是两回事。
posts.text_en: I have read Fehr's experiments and I respect them. But note the magnitudes: a few hundred students, stakes of a few dozen dollars, one afternoon. **What changes behaviour in a real market is price elasticity, not a situational cue in a laboratory — and the people on a waiting list are not subjects.** After Iran permitted compensated kidney donation its waiting list essentially disappeared: that is two decades of field evidence, not one small sample. As for crowding out, I grant that it exists, but it has conditions — it shows up most clearly when the sum is small enough to be read as an insult. Offering a decent price and tossing someone a coin are not the same act.

glossary.价格弹性: price elasticity（价格弹性）：数量对价格变动的反应程度。贝克尔一系认为，只要供给对价格有弹性，允许付费就能把短缺变成充足，这是主张禁令的一方最难回避的实证问题。

glossary_en.price elasticity: How strongly quantity responds to a change in price. The Chicago argument is that wherever supply is elastic, permitting payment converts a shortage into an adequate supply — the empirical point hardest for prohibitionists to evade.

posts.text: 努斯鲍姆女士把问题从「象征的不洁」挪到「真实的伤害与选择」，这一步我赞成。可你那张清单里最要命的一条被轻轻放过了：**能不能退出，从来不是个人品质，而是账户余额。**一个手上还有半年房租的人说「我自愿」，与一个下周就要被扫地出门的人说同一句话，是两种语言。你把它叫作议价地位不平等，我称之为阶级。既然如此，检验一个市场正当与否的办法很简单：让所有卖家先真的拥有拒绝的能力，再看还剩多少人愿意卖。
posts.text_en: Professor Nussbaum moves the question from symbolic impurity to real harm and real choice, and I welcome that step. But the decisive item on your checklist slips past too lightly. **Whether a person can exit is never a matter of character; it is a matter of the balance in the account.** Someone with six months' rent in hand who says 'I consent' and someone facing eviction next week who says the same words are speaking two different languages. You call this unequal bargaining power; I call it class. In which case the test of a market's legitimacy is simple: give every seller a genuine capacity to refuse first, then see how many are still willing to sell.

glossary.阶级: class（阶级）：马克思用来指人在生产资料占有关系中的位置。他认为个人的『自愿』受这一位置约束：不占有生产资料的人必须出卖劳动力才能活下去，其同意的自由度与占有者不可同日而语。

glossary_en.class: Marx's term for a person's position in the ownership of the means of production. He held that individual 'consent' is bounded by that position: those who own no means of production must sell their labour-power to live, so the freedom of their agreement is not comparable to an owner's.

posts.text: 弗里德曼子曰：禁之，则贫者失其一途。此言似仁而实薄。夫使人至于鬻肾以偿屋租者，非其人不智，乃上下交征利而民无以自立也。今不去其所以致贫者，而曰吾更与汝一途以自赎，是纵火而后鬻水，犹自谓有恩于人。且君子有所不为，而后可以有为；国有所不市，非独为贫者计，亦所以立一国之节也。**故为政者当先使民有恒产，而后议其可鬻与否。**
posts.text_en: Master Friedman says: ban it, and the poor lose one of their paths. The words sound humane and are in fact thin. That a man is reduced to selling a kidney to pay his rent is not because he lacks sense; it is because high and low alike grasp at profit until ordinary people cannot stand on their own. You do not touch what made him poor, and instead announce that you are granting him one more path by which to redeem himself. That is setting the fire and then selling water, while calling yourself a benefactor. Besides, a gentleman first has things he will not do, and only then is capable of doing anything; a state first has things it will not put on the stall, and only then has a character of its own — which is not merely a calculation on behalf of the poor. **So those who govern should first see that the people have a settled livelihood, and argue afterwards about what may be sold.**
posts.vernacular: 弗里德曼说：一禁，穷人就少了一条路。这话听着仁厚，其实很薄。一个人沦落到卖肾去还房租，不是他笨，是因为上上下下都在争利，普通人立不住脚。你不去动那个让他变穷的东西，只对他说「我再给你一条自赎的路」，那等于先放火、再卖水，还说自己对人有恩。何况君子先有不肯做的事，然后才谈得上有所作为；一个国家先有不摆上摊的东西，才立得起自己的规矩，这不只是替穷人打算。**所以当政的人该先让百姓有稳定的产业与生计，再来讨论什么能卖、什么不能卖。**

glossary.恒产: constant means of support（恒产）：孟子的政治经济主张。他认为百姓若无稳定的田产与生计（恒产），就难有稳定的道德自持（恒心）；因此仁政的第一步是制民之产，而不是先要求百姓守德。

glossary_en.a settled livelihood: Mencius's political-economic thesis: without settled property and a stable means of support, ordinary people cannot be expected to hold a settled heart. Hence the first act of humane government is to secure the people's livelihood, not to demand virtue of them first.

posts.text: 桑德尔画一线，曰此线之内不可市。老僧问：此线亦在市中否？**汝以「神圣」为一物而守之，则已将它作可持之资，与商人无异。**梁武帝造寺无数，所求者「功德」一件耳，故达摩答以实无。今人守清白如守宝，一旦有人出高价，其心先动，价未议而守已破矣。是故非卖之物不在名单上，而在应无所住而生其心一语中。名单非不可立，然立之者当自知：所守者非彼物，乃此心不为价所转耳。
posts.text_en: Sandel draws a line and says: inside this line, nothing may be traded. This old monk asks — is the line itself not also inside the market? **By guarding 'the sacred' as a thing, you have already made it an asset you hold, which is no different from a merchant's stock.** Emperor Wu built temples beyond counting, and what he was after was one item called merit; hence Bodhidharma's answer that there was none. People today guard a clean name as they would a treasure, and the moment a high price appears the heart has already moved — the terms are not yet discussed and the guard is already broken. So what is not for sale is not on any list; it is in the line 'let the mind arise without abiding anywhere.' A list may certainly be drawn up, but whoever draws it should know: what you are guarding is not that thing, but a mind that a price cannot turn.
posts.vernacular: 桑德尔画一条线，说线内的东西不可买卖。我问一句：这条线本身，是不是也在市场里？**你把「神圣」当成一件东西守着，那它就已经成了你可以持有的资产，跟商人手里的货没有分别。**梁武帝造了无数寺庙，图的不过是「功德」这一件货，所以达摩答他：实在没有。今天有人把清白当宝贝守着，一旦有人出个高价，心先动了——价还没谈，守就已经破了。所以真正不卖的东西不在清单上，而在「应无所住而生其心」这句话里。清单不是不能立，但立清单的人要明白：你守的不是那件东西，是这颗心不被价格牵着走。

glossary.应无所住而生其心: let the mind arise without abiding anywhere（应无所住而生其心）：出自《金刚经》，相传慧能听闻此句而开悟。意为不把心固着在任何一个对象上——包括『神圣』『清白』这些好东西——心才不被所执之物牵动。

glossary_en.let the mind arise without abiding anywh: A line from the Diamond Sutra on hearing which, by tradition, Huineng awakened. It means not fixing the mind upon any object — including good objects such as 'the sacred' or 'a clean name' — so that the mind is not pulled about by what it grasps.

posts.text: 桑德尔，我同意有些边界该守，但你的「腐蚀」论证有一段不体面的家史。「这种事拿钱换就脏了」——这句话历史上最常落在谁头上？演员、乐师、接生婆、护士，以及女人的几乎一切劳动。它从不追问她们过得好不好，只追问她们看上去洁不洁；这套语言把物化的指控扣在了被物化的人身上。**当一个论证的结论永远指向同一批人的耻辱，就该怀疑它测量的不是道德，而是等级。**我要求把每条禁令拆成可查的问题：谁受伤、伤多重、议价地位如何、有没有更好的替代。答不上来，那条线就不该由法律来划。
posts.text_en: Sandel, I agree that some boundaries are worth keeping, but your corruption argument has a disreputable family history. 'It becomes dirty once money changes hands' — on whom has that sentence most often landed? Actors, musicians, midwives, nurses, and very nearly all the labour of women. It never asks how they are faring, only whether they look clean; the vocabulary lays the charge of objectification at the feet of the people being objectified. **When an argument's conclusion always points to the shame of the same group, we should suspect it is measuring rank rather than morality.** I want every prohibition broken down into checkable questions: who is harmed, how badly, how unequal is the bargaining position, is there a better alternative. If those cannot be answered, the law has no business drawing the line.

glossary.物化: objectification（物化）：把人当作工具、可替换之物或纯粹的身体来对待。努斯鲍姆细分出多种不同含义，并指出其中有些在特定关系中未必有害，关键在于是否否认了对方的自主与主体性。

glossary_en.objectification: Treating a person as an instrument, as fungible, or as mere body. Nussbaum distinguishes several distinct senses and argues that some are not necessarily harmful within particular relationships; what matters is whether the other's autonomy and subjectivity are denied.

posts.text: 贝克尔，价格弹性我同意，伊朗的等待名单也确实缩短了。但请把另一半数据一起读：对伊朗供肾者的随访研究里，多数人事后表示后悔，相当比例报告健康与就业状况变差，而他们几乎全部来自最低收入群体。**你消除的不是短缺，你把短缺从等待名单转移到了另一群人的身体上——这一次不上榜，所以不算死亡。**我并不主张一禁了之。我主张凡是要开的市场，先规定谁能卖、给多少、事后由谁负责随访，把可测量的伤害写进制度，而不是写进良心。
posts.text_en: Becker, I accept price elasticity, and Iran's waiting list did indeed shrink. But read the other half of the data with it: follow-up studies of Iranian kidney vendors find that most report regret, a substantial share report worse health and worse employment afterwards, and almost all of them come from the lowest income group. **You did not eliminate the shortage; you moved it off the waiting list and into another group of people's bodies — and this time it appears on no list, so it does not count as a death.** I am not arguing for prohibition. I am arguing that any market you open must specify in advance who may sell, at what price, and who is responsible for following them up afterwards — writing measurable harm into the institution rather than into someone's conscience.

posts.text: 我的结论是把这场辩论从形容词换成清单——不是禁售清单，是核查清单。要判断一项交易该不该被允许，问五件可查的事：她有没有真实的替代选项；能不能在事后退出；身体完整与健康有没有制度保障；议价地位差多少，能否用集体谈判或最低条款补上；这项活动会不会把一群人推进被歧视的位置。**答得上来，就该管制而不是禁止；答不上来，那条线更可能是在维护体面，而不是在保护人。**落到个人身上也一样：遇到「这事不该拿钱换」的直觉，先把它翻译成「谁会受伤、伤多重」；翻译不出来，就先按下不表。签任何拿身体或时间换钱的合同——加班、夜班、试药、跑单——先看退出条款和事后保障，那两页比薪资那一行更决定你的处境。最后，别用一件事收不收费去判断一个人体不体面，那从来不是一把准的尺。
posts.text_en: My conclusion is to replace the adjectives in this debate with a list — not a list of prohibitions but a checklist. To judge whether a transaction should be permitted, ask five checkable things. Does she have a real alternative? Can she exit afterwards? Are bodily integrity and health institutionally protected? How wide is the gap in bargaining power, and can collective bargaining or a floor of minimum terms close it? And will the activity push a group of people into a position of being despised? **If those can be answered, regulate rather than prohibit; if they cannot, the line is more likely defending respectability than protecting anyone.** The same applies to individuals. When the intuition 'this should not be exchanged for money' arrives, translate it into who is harmed and how badly; if it will not translate, set it aside for now. Before signing any contract that trades your body or your time — overtime, night shifts, drug trials, delivery work — read the exit clause and the after-the-fact protections, since those two pages decide your situation more than the line stating your pay. And never judge a person's respectability by whether they charge for something; that has never been an accurate ruler.

posts.text: 我保留我的方法，但接受一条修正：价格能完成配置，配置不等于正当。所以我把结论收窄——**凡是短缺会直接要人命、而供给对价格确有反应的领域，一禁了之在道德上并不中立，它有一份看不见的账单。**器官如此，疫苗与关键药品的产能也如此。但费尔的随访数据说服了我一件事：开市场的同时必须把卖方的后半生写进合同，否则你只是把风险外包给了最没能力承担的人。给普通人两条：一，做家庭大决定时，把不花钱的选项也标上价——你辞职陪床的那三个月，机会成本是真实存在的，看清楚了才不会日后互相埋怨；二，凡是有人对你说「这不是钱的问题」，多半正是钱的问题，只是有人不愿意让它被算清楚。
posts.text_en: I keep my method but accept one amendment: price can complete an allocation, and an allocation is not thereby just. So I narrow my conclusion. **Wherever a shortage kills directly and supply does respond to price, a flat prohibition is not morally neutral — it carries an invisible bill.** That holds for organs, and for vaccine and essential-drug capacity too. But Fehr's follow-up data have convinced me of one thing: any market you open must write the seller's later life into the contract, or you have merely outsourced the risk to those least able to bear it. Two suggestions for ordinary readers. First, when making a large family decision, put a price on the unpaid options too — the three months you took off to sit at a bedside have a real opportunity cost, and seeing it clearly is what prevents recrimination later. Second, when someone tells you 'this isn't about money', it usually is about money; someone simply prefers that it not be counted.

posts.text: 诸位吵了三轮清单，我只留一句：**清单是结果，不是原因；只要有人不卖就活不下去，你写多长的禁售名单都拦不住他，只会把交易赶到更暗的地方去。**费尔的随访数据正是我的论据：卖肾的几乎全部来自最低收入群体，这不是巧合，是结构。所以真正该被追问的不是「器官能不能卖」，而是为什么医疗、住房、教育这三样在许多地方本身就是商品，逼得人拿身体去补差额。我给普通人的建议不是道德修养。先弄清你的收入里有多大比例是靠出卖时间换来的，再看看有没有一样东西是你不靠出卖时间也能积累的。别一个人去议价——单独的人永远是价格接受者，凡是能加入的集体谈判、行业组织、业主委员会都值得加入。至于「我是自愿的」这句话，留到你真有第二个选项的时候再说。
posts.text_en: You have quarrelled for three rounds over a list, and I will leave one sentence behind. **The list is an effect, not a cause: so long as there are people who cannot live unless they sell, no length of prohibition will stop them — it will only drive the trade somewhere darker.** Fehr's follow-up data are my evidence: nearly every kidney vendor comes from the lowest income group, which is not coincidence but structure. So the real question is not whether organs may be sold, but why health care, housing and education are themselves commodities in so many places, forcing people to make up the difference with their bodies. My suggestions are not exercises in virtue. Work out what share of your income comes from selling your time, then look for anything you can accumulate without selling it. Never bargain alone — a lone individual is always a price-taker, so any collective bargaining unit, trade body or tenants' association worth joining is worth joining. And save the sentence 'I did this voluntarily' for when you genuinely had a second option.

posts.text: 我不否认费尔的挤出效应，也不回避伊朗的随访数据难看。但请注意，那些数据讲的是市场设计得糟，不是市场不该存在——没有合同、没有随访、没有事后保障，本来就是半个黑市。**真正的对照组从来不是理想国，而是禁令之下的现状：中介、器官旅游，以及一份没有人替他们统计的死亡名单。**给普通人三条。第一，别把「我讨厌」和「应该禁止」混为一谈；你只能替自己不买，要替别人禁，得先拿出他被伤害的证据。第二，凡是你靠意志力硬扛的事，就给它配一个可执行的价格：健身年卡不如按次退款，戒烟不如先押一笔钱在朋友那儿。第三，谈薪水、谈房租、谈家里谁做什么，把价钱和分工说清楚——含糊的人情往往比明码标价更贵，只是账单来得晚。
posts.text_en: I do not deny Fehr's crowding-out, nor do I dodge how ugly the Iranian follow-up data are. But notice what those data show: a badly designed market, not a market that ought not exist. No contract, no follow-up, no post-hoc protection — that is half a black market to begin with. **The relevant control group is never utopia; it is the status quo under prohibition: brokers, transplant tourism, and a death list nobody bothers to compile.** Three suggestions. First, do not confuse 'I find it distasteful' with 'it should be banned'; you may decline to buy for yourself, but to ban it for others you must produce evidence of harm. Second, wherever you are relying on willpower, attach an enforceable price instead: a per-session refund beats an annual gym membership, and money deposited with a friend beats a resolution to quit smoking. Third, in negotiating salary, rent, or who does what at home, state the price and the division plainly — vague goodwill is usually more expensive than a posted rate; the bill simply arrives later.

posts.text: 我把可测量的部分收个尾。第一，钱与动机不是相加关系：**同一笔钱，被理解成感谢时会加强合作，被理解成定价时会替换掉它，差别常常只在怎么说、由谁说、附不附条件。**第二，市场情境本身会改变人——法尔克与谢赫的结果说明，把同一个道德决定放进买卖框架里，愿意成交的人会变多，因为责任被分摊进了「反正别人也会做」。第三，挤出大多可逆但不对称：撤掉一项报酬之后，自愿水平往往回不到原来的高度。所以我的建议很具体。家人朋友的帮忙别付现金，改成回请或送东西——同样的价值，一个走市场账户，一个走关系账户。要奖励孩子或下属，就奖励过程与难度，别给每件小事挂单价。而凡是你想长期做下去的事，先确认它有一个不靠报酬也成立的理由，然后再谈钱。
posts.text_en: Let me close on the measurable part. First, money and motivation do not simply add up: **the same sum strengthens cooperation when it is read as thanks and displaces it when it is read as a price — and the difference often lies only in how it is said, by whom, and with what conditions attached.** Second, the market frame itself changes people: Falk and Szech show that placing the same moral decision inside a buying-and-selling frame produces more takers, because responsibility gets diluted into 'somebody else would have done it anyway'. Third, crowding out is mostly reversible but asymmetric: withdraw a payment and voluntary effort rarely climbs back to where it began. So my advice is concrete. Do not pay cash for help from family and friends — reciprocate with a meal or a gift; the same value travels down a market account in one case and a relationship account in the other. When rewarding a child or a subordinate, reward the process and the difficulty rather than posting a unit price on every small task. And before anything you intend to keep doing for years, make sure it has a reason that holds without the payment — only then talk about money.

posts.text: 三轮既毕，吾说不改：市可存，而心有不可市者。**民之为道也，有恒产者有恒心，无恒产而有恒心者，惟士为能。**故善为政者不责民以圣，而先制其产；产既定，然后教之以义，则鬻身之事自寡。至于诸君所争之列，吾以四事验之：一曰其人别有他途否，二曰其事伤身否，三曰其价可议否，四曰行之既久而风俗厚薄何如。四者皆善，则市之可也；有一不善，则缓之、限之、监之。若夫居家，则父子夫妇之间勿以钱结算——一结算则恩尽而计生，虽日日算得其平，而家已非家矣。
posts.text_en: Three rounds are done and I do not change my case: let there be markets, and let there be that in the heart which is not for market. **As to the way of the people: those with a settled livelihood have a settled heart; to have a settled heart without a settled livelihood is possible only for the scholar.** Therefore good government does not demand sainthood of the people but first secures their living; once their living is secure, teach them righteousness, and the selling of one's own body will grow rare of itself. As for the list you have been arguing over, I test it four ways. Does the person have another road? Does the act injure the body? Can the price be negotiated? And after long practice, do the customs of the place grow richer or thinner? If all four answer well, let it be traded; if one does not, then delay it, cap it, supervise it. And at home: between parent and child, husband and wife, do not settle accounts in money — settle accounts and affection ends where reckoning begins; you may balance the books daily and the household is no longer a household.
posts.vernacular: 三轮下来，我的说法不变：市场可以有，但人心里有不该拿去交易的东西。**百姓过日子的道理是：有稳定的产业与生计，才有稳定的操守；没有恒产还能守住恒心的，只有读书人做得到。**所以会治理的人不要求百姓个个是圣人，而是先让他们有稳定的产业；产业定了，再教他们讲道义，卖身求生的事自然就少了。至于诸位争的那张清单，我用四件事来验：第一，这个人还有没有别的路；第二，这件事伤不伤身体；第三，这个价钱他能不能议；第四，长期做下去，一地的风气是变厚还是变薄。四条都过得去，就开；有一条过不去，就缓一缓、限一限、盯紧一点。至于家里，父子之间、夫妻之间别拿钱结算——一结算，情分就到头了、算计就起来了；哪怕天天算得公平，那个家也已经不是家了。

glossary.恒心: a settled heart（恒心）：孟子与『恒产』相对而言的道德稳定性。他认为除少数以修身为业者外，一般人在生计动荡时难以持守德行，因此把百姓的操守问题首先看作制度与生计问题。

glossary_en.a settled heart: In Mencius, the moral steadiness paired with a settled livelihood. He held that apart from the few who make self-cultivation their vocation, ordinary people cannot maintain virtue amid economic instability — which makes popular morality first of all a question of institutions and livelihoods.

posts.text: 三轮下来我承认两件事：弗里德曼说得对，禁令有代价，而这代价常由最穷的人承担；努斯鲍姆说得对，「玷污」这个词背后有一段该被清算的历史。但核心我不撤回：**判断一个市场该不该开，得先问这件好东西的意义何在、什么样的分配方式与它相称，而不是一上来就问它值多少钱。**器官、代孕、选票、兵役、公民身份之所以难，是因为它们同时牵着两根线：一根是穷人被迫的可能，一根是这件事本身会被改写。落到日常上：家里的事别急着用钱结算——孩子的成绩、老人的陪伴、朋友的帮忙，一旦换成价目表，就再也换不回来。听到「反正大家都出得起价」，请追问一句谁出不起。而每当有人提议把一样人人有份的东西改成按出价排序，那一票值得你投反对。
posts.text_en: After three rounds I concede two things. Friedman is right that prohibitions have costs, and that those costs usually fall on the poorest. Nussbaum is right that the word 'defilement' carries a history that deserves an audit. But I do not withdraw the core: **to judge whether a market should be opened, ask first what the good is for and what mode of distribution befits it — not what it is worth.** Organs, surrogacy, votes, military service and citizenship are hard precisely because two threads run through them at once: the possibility that the poor are compelled, and the possibility that the thing itself gets rewritten. As for daily life: do not settle domestic matters in cash — a child's grades, an elderly parent's company, a friend's help; once converted into a price list they do not convert back. When you hear 'everyone can afford it anyway', ask who cannot. And whenever someone proposes to convert something everyone holds equally into something ranked by willingness to pay, that is a vote worth casting against.

posts.text: 诸君条列所禁，勤矣。老僧不废其事，然有一言相赠：**禁在外，守在内；外禁可越，内守不移。**心已随价而动者，纵天下皆禁，亦必于暗处求之；心不随价者，虽万金当前，亦如风过耳。故功夫不在拟一张不卖之单，而在遇价之时看自己那一念从何处起：是惧，是贪，是不得已。三者各有对治——惧者先足其生，贪者先减其欲，不得已者众人当助之。日用中亦有可行者：凡一事将以钱了之，先自问一句——此事以钱了之，明日尚在否？在，则市之无妨；不在，则钱虽入手，其物已失。
posts.text_en: You gentlemen itemise what may not be sold, and diligently so. This old monk does not dismiss the work, but offers one line: **prohibition is outside, keeping is within; an outer ban can be crossed, an inner keeping does not move.** A heart already moved by the price will seek the thing in the dark though the whole world forbids it; a heart unmoved by price hears ten thousand in gold as wind passing the ear. So the practice is not in drafting a list of what may not be sold, but in watching, at the moment the price appears, where that first thought comes from: fear, greed, or having no choice. Each has its remedy — for fear, first secure the living; for greed, first reduce the wanting; for one with no choice, the rest of us should help. There is something usable in daily life too. Whenever you are about to settle a matter with money, ask first: settled this way, will the thing still be there tomorrow? If it will, trade freely. If it will not, then the money is in hand and the thing is already gone.
posts.vernacular: 诸位一条条列出不许卖的东西，很勤勉。我不否定这件事，但送一句话：**禁令在外面，守在里面；外面的禁令可以绕过去，里面的守却不会动。**心已经被价钱牵动的人，就算天下都禁了，他也会到暗处去求；心不被价钱牵动的人，万两黄金摆在面前，也像风从耳边过。所以功夫不在拟一张不卖清单，而在价格出现的那一刻，看自己第一个念头从哪儿起：是怕，是贪，还是实在没办法。三样各有各的解法——怕的，先把生计安顿好；贪的，先把欲望减下去；实在没办法的，旁人该搭把手。日常里也有可用的：凡是一件事你打算用钱了结，先问自己一句——用钱了结之后，这件事明天还在不在？在，那就买卖无妨；不在，那钱虽然到手，东西已经没了。

summaries.summary: 全场的最大共识出乎意料地整齐：没有人主张什么都能卖，也没有人愿意只凭「恶心」就下禁令。**八个人最后都落在同一处——真正决定一桩买卖正不正当的，不是钱本身，而是卖方有没有退路、这件事会不会因此被改写。**分歧在三处展开。一是判据：桑德尔要问这样好东西的意义与相称的分配方式，努斯鲍姆坚持只认可查的伤害与议价地位，指出「玷污」的历史大多落在女人与低阶职业头上。二是禁令的对照组：弗里德曼与贝克尔说是黑市与等待名单，马克思说是被制造出来的贫困。三是着力点：孟子与慧能把它放回恒产与那一念，其余人放在制度。
summaries.insight: 有一侧几乎没被审视：**全场都在问谁被迫卖，却没人问买得起的人被改造成了什么样。**一个习惯用钱绕开所有不便的人——插队、代排、代跑腿、代陪诊、代照顾父母——买走的不只是时间，还有与别人共处同一条队伍的经验。而正是那点共处，维持着他对公共事物好坏的利害感。这解释了一个常见现象：越是能买到私人替代品的人，越不在意公立医院、公办学校与公共交通烂成什么样，因为那些队伍已经与他无关。所以市场边界最实用的一条检验也许不在卖方而在买方：这桩交易会不会让付得起的人从某个共同处境里悄悄退出。
summaries.advice: 先做一件反直觉的事：挑一件你惯常用钱绕开的公共不便，本周亲自去经历一次——排一次队、坐一趟公交、自己跑一趟窗口。这不是苦行，是把你对公共品质的判断力接回来。第二，把家人朋友之间的帮忙移出现金结算，改成回请、送东西或轮流搭手；同样的价值，走关系账户比走市场账户更耐用，一旦付了现金往往就回不去了。第三，凡要签下拿身体或时间换钱的合同——加班、夜班、试药、跑单、代驾——先翻退出条款与事后保障，**那两页比薪资那一行更决定你的处境。**第四，遇到「这事不该拿钱换」的直觉，先翻译成「谁受伤、伤多重」；翻不出来，就先别急着替别人下禁令。
summaries.summary_en: The largest area of agreement was unexpectedly tidy: nobody argued that everything may be sold, and nobody was willing to prohibit anything on the strength of disgust alone. **All eight ended up in the same place — what settles the legitimacy of a transaction is not the money but whether the seller has a way out, and whether the thing itself gets rewritten in the process.** The disagreements open at three points. On criteria: Sandel wants to ask what the good is for and what mode of distribution befits it, while Nussbaum will accept only demonstrable harm and bargaining position, noting that the charge of defilement has historically landed on women and low-status trades. On the control group for prohibition: Friedman and Becker name the black market and the waiting list, Marx names manufactured poverty. And on where the lever sits: Mencius and Huineng put it back in livelihood and in the first movement of the mind, the rest in institutions.
summaries.insight_en: One side of this went almost unexamined. **The room asked at length who is compelled to sell, and never asked what buying does to those who can afford it.** Someone accustomed to paying their way around every inconvenience — the queue, the errand, the wait at a clinic, the care of a parent — purchases more than time; they also buy their way out of standing in the same line as everybody else. And it is precisely that shared standing which sustains their stake in whether public things are any good. It explains a familiar pattern: those best able to buy private substitutes care least how badly the public hospital, the state school or the bus network is run, because those queues no longer concern them. So perhaps the most usable test of a market's limits lies not with the seller but with the buyer: does this transaction quietly let those who can pay withdraw from a shared condition?
summaries.advice_en: Start with something counter-intuitive: pick one public inconvenience you habitually pay your way around and go through it yourself this week — stand in the queue, take the bus, deal with the counter in person. This is not asceticism; it reconnects your judgement about whether public things are working. Second, move help between family and friends out of cash settlement and into a return invitation, a gift, or taking turns; the same value lasts better travelling down a relationship account than a market account, and once cash has been paid the route is hard to reverse. Third, before signing anything that trades your body or your time — overtime, night shifts, drug trials, delivery or driving work — read the exit clause and the after-the-fact protections; **those two pages decide your situation more than the line stating your pay.** Fourth, when the intuition 'this should not be exchanged for money' arrives, translate it into who is harmed and how badly; if it will not translate, hold off on prohibiting it for someone else.

summaries.summary: 这场最值得带走的共识，不是“市场好或坏”，而是没有一种分配方式是免费的：价格有账单，禁令也有账单；自愿要看退路，尊严也要看制度。**真正的问题不是钱能不能出现，而是钱一出现，会不会改变人、物和关系的性质，并把代价推给最弱者。**分歧在于判准：有人先看意义与公民伦理，有人先看伤害证据与可行能力，有人先看短缺和效率，有人追问贫困结构本身。
summaries.insight: “能不能卖”问得太早，很多争议更该先问“卖了以后能不能修复”。一顿饭、一小时代排、一次咨询，大多可逆；一颗肾、一次代孕、一次投票、被长期量化的亲密关系，却会留下难以撤销的身体、身份或信任后果。**越不可逆、越难由本人独自承受后果的交易，越不能只靠当下同意和一次性价格来正当化。**这把问题从抽象禁忌拉回制度：冷静期、退出权、终身保障、公共审查，都是让“同意”不至于太廉价的装置。
summaries.advice: 今天就能做三件事。第一，给自己列一张“两栏清单”：哪些事可明码标价，哪些事只适合感谢、互助或轮流承担，先写家庭照护、朋友帮忙、加班、借钱。第二，签任何消耗身体或时间的合同时，逐项查退路：能否拒绝、能否退出、谁付后续风险。第三，遇到公共争议，别只问禁不禁，追问补偿、监管和替代保障。**先把拒绝的能力做出来，再谈自愿，判断会稳很多。**
summaries.summary_en: The most useful shared ground here is not that markets are good or bad; it is that no allocation method is morally free. Prices leave a bill, bans leave a bill, consent depends on real alternatives, and dignity needs institutions rather than slogans. **The real question is not whether money appears, but whether its appearance changes the good, the person, or the relationship, and shifts the cost onto those least able to bear it.** The disagreement is over the test: should we begin with the meaning of the good and civic equality, with measurable harm and capabilities, with scarcity and incentives, or with the poverty and power relations that make people sell in the first place?
summaries.insight_en: Whether something may be sold is often the second question; the first is whether the damage can be repaired after the sale. A meal, an hour of waiting in line, or a professional consultation is usually reversible. A kidney, a pregnancy contract, a vote, or a relationship that has been turned into a permanent ledger is not. **The less reversible a transaction is, and the less the seller can personally absorb its downstream risks, the less it can be justified by one moment of consent and one lump-sum price.** That reframes the debate in practical terms: cooling-off periods, exit rights, lifelong medical coverage, independent advice, and public review are not bureaucratic clutter. They are ways of making consent less cheap.
summaries.advice_en: Do three things this week. First, make a two-column list: which things in your life can be priced openly, and which should be handled through gratitude, reciprocity, or shared duty. Start with caregiving, favors from friends, overtime, and loans. Second, before signing any contract that spends your body or your time, check the exit route: can you refuse, can you quit, and who pays for later harm? Third, in public debates, do not stop at ban or allow; ask what compensation, supervision, and alternatives exist. **Build the real ability to say no first; only then does talk of voluntary choice become reliable.**

summaries.summary: 最大的共识是：毫无边界的市场极其危险，而『穷人的脆弱性』是检验任何市场合法性的底线。马克思对阶级结构的拷问、孟子的『先制恒产』、贝克尔强调的事后保障、努斯鲍姆的弱势群体自决权，指向的是同一句：在极端不平等的处境下，单纯的『自愿成交』没有道德说服力。分歧在于如何应对这种脆弱性。一方（弗里德曼、贝克尔、努斯鲍姆）主张用更优的制度设计、底线保障与直接的财富转移来完善市场，把价格视作解决稀缺的最优解；另一方（桑德尔、费尔）则坚信，**价格绝非中立的分配工具，而是一种会改写人类社会关系与道德动机的『基因编辑技术』**——某些事物一旦被标价，其内在价值便不可逆转地坍塌。
summaries.insight: 算法时代的注意力与隐私，是这场古典辩论的最大盲区。诸位讨论的都是看得见的买卖——器官、代排队、有偿代孕；而数字经济里最庞大的那笔交易是在无形中完成的：用户没有付钱，却在不断出让自己的行为偏好、社交网络、情绪乃至潜意识反应，换取『免费』的服务。**当交易被『免费体验』的糖衣包裹、变得不可见时，关于『能否退出』与『议价地位』的那张核查清单就整个失效了。**现代社会的危险不再只是富人买走穷人的肾脏，而是每个人的数字生命特征被系统性地转化为最值钱的商品；这种隐性市场对个人主权的侵蚀，比明码标价的买卖更深远，也更难防。
summaries.advice: 结合诸位思想家的智慧与现代数字生活，你可以立刻采取以下行动：第一，执行费尔与桑德尔的“账户隔离原则”。**在家庭和亲密关系中，凡是需要用人情和爱维系的事情，坚决不要用现金结算**，务必用礼物、一顿用心的晚餐或对等的陪伴时间来替代。第二，应用努斯鲍姆的“退出测试”。在接下任何一份用健康或极致的时间换取金钱的工作（如极限加班、试药、高风险外包）前，先查阅合同里的退出条款和事后医疗保障；如果无法随时止损，这笔钱就不该赚。第三，审查并夺回你的数字资产。今天就关掉手机里非必要App的“个性化广告推荐”和精准位置追踪，拒绝在不知情的情况下将自己的心智与注意力免费挂在市场上出售。
summaries.summary_en: The most significant consensus across the panel is that an utterly boundaryless market is dangerous, and the vulnerability of the poor is the ultimate litmus test for any market's legitimacy. Whether through Marx's critique of structural inequality, Mencius's emphasis on basic livelihoods, Becker's call for safety nets, or Nussbaum's focus on agency, everyone agrees that desperation inherently invalidates 'voluntary' consent. However, the true divergence emerges in how to address this vulnerability. One side (Friedman, Becker, Nussbaum) believes we should refine market mechanisms through better institutional design, baseline guarantees, and direct wealth transfers, viewing price as the optimal tool for scarcity. The other side (Sandel, Fehr) insists that **price is never a neutral allocation tool, but rather a 'gene-editing technology' that fundamentally rewrites human social relations and moral motivations.** For the latter, pricing certain goods causes an irreversible collapse of their intrinsic value.
summaries.insight_en: Attention and privacy in the algorithmic age constitute the biggest blind spot in this classical debate. The panelists discussed highly visible transactions (organs, queuing, surrogacy), but in the digital economy, the most profound trades are entirely invisible. Users pay no money, yet constantly sell their behavioral preferences, emotional states, and subconscious reactions in exchange for 'free' services. **When transactions are sugarcoated as 'free experiences' and become invisible, classical checklists regarding 'voluntary exit' and 'bargaining power' completely fail.** The danger of modern society is no longer just the rich buying kidneys from the poor, but the systemic transformation of everyone's digital biometric data into highly lucrative commodities. We engage in countless imperceptible micro-transactions daily; this hidden market's erosion of personal sovereignty and free will is far deeper and harder to guard against than explicitly priced trades.
summaries.advice_en: Combining the wisdom of these thinkers with modern digital realities, here are actions you can take immediately: First, implement Fehr and Sandel's 'account isolation principle.' **In family and intimate relationships, never use cash to settle favors that rely on love and connection**; instead, reciprocate with thoughtful gifts, a homemade dinner, or equivalent quality time. Second, apply Nussbaum's 'exit test.' Before accepting any job that trades your health or extreme amounts of time for high pay (e.g., extreme overtime, clinical trials), thoroughly review the exit clauses and post-employment health guarantees. If you cannot cut your losses at any time, it's not worth the money. Third, audit and reclaim your digital assets. Turn off 'personalized ad tracking' and precise location services on non-essential apps today, refusing to unknowingly put your attention and psychological profile up for sale.

hooks.text: **退出权，也许比一张禁售清单更管用**：三轮里真正把两边分开的，不是「能不能卖」，而是「卖了之后能不能反悔」。如果所有拿身体与时间换钱的交易都必须配上冷静期、可撤销条款与长期随访，禁售清单还剩下多少非划不可的项目？又有哪几样是无论怎么加保障，都仍然不该开的？
hooks.text_en: **A right of exit may do more work than a list of prohibitions**: what actually separated the two sides across three rounds was not whether a thing may be sold but whether the seller can change their mind afterwards. If every transaction that trades body or time had to carry a cooling-off period, a revocable clause and long-term follow-up, how many items would still have to be on the prohibited list? And which few should stay closed no matter how many protections are bolted on?

hooks.text: **这件事能不能安全地标价？一张自测表**：全场都同意价格会改变被标价的东西，却没人说清哪些事经得起标价、哪些一标就散。与其记住一份清单，不如手上有一套能自己用的判据——它靠什么运转，决定了钱进来之后它还在不在。
hooks.text_en: **Can this be safely priced? A self-test**: everyone agreed that a price changes what it is applied to, yet nobody spelled out which things survive being priced and which fall apart on contact. Better than memorising a list is holding a test you can run yourself — what a thing runs on determines whether it is still there once money arrives.

answer.lead: **一件事能不能安全地标价，取决于它靠什么运转。**下面五问，任答一个「是」，就说明标价会改变这件事本身，该换一种方式结算。

head: 自测题
答「是」意味着什么
该怎么办
rows: 这件事的意义，有一部分来自「他是出于心意做的」吗？
标价把心意换成对价，收到的人第一反应会去算你付了多少
改用回请、送东西、轮流搭手，别付现金
做这件事的人，本来就有一个不靠报酬也成立的理由吗？
外在报酬容易把内在理由替换掉，而撤掉报酬后往往回不到原点
只奖励过程与难度，别给每件小事挂单价
卖方是不是根本没有第二个选项？
价格衡量的不再是这东西值多少，而是他有多急
先补上退路（借款、救助、保险、公共托底），再谈交易
交易会不会用掉卖方难以恢复的东西——器官、健康、一段不可逆的时间？
这是一次性、不可撤销的支付，事后没有纠错机会
设冷静期、数量上限与长期随访，或干脆不开
按出价分配，会不会改变这样东西所代表的身份——选票、荣誉、公民权、判决？
它的价值本来就靠「不能买」撑着，买到手的已不是原物
维持人人一份或按资格分配，根本不要开价

answer.tail: 两条原则收束：**一，靠「他本来就愿意」运转的事别标价；靠「稀缺必须分配」运转的事，标价往往比排队更公平也更透明。**二，实在要标价，就把退出条款与事后保障写在价格前面——那两行比金额更决定结果。

answer_en.lead: **Whether something can be safely priced depends on what it runs on.** Answer 'yes' to any one of the five below and pricing will change the thing itself, so settle it another way.

head: Self-test
What a 'yes' means
What to do instead
rows: Does part of the meaning come from the fact that they did it willingly?
A price converts goodwill into consideration; the recipient's first instinct becomes to work out what you paid
Reciprocate with an invitation, a gift or taking turns — not cash
Does the person already have a reason to do it that holds without payment?
External reward tends to displace the internal reason, and removing it rarely restores the original level
Reward the process and the difficulty; do not post a unit price on every small task
Does the seller in fact have no second option?
The price no longer measures what the thing is worth, only how urgently they need it
Restore a way out first — credit, relief, insurance, a public floor — then discuss the trade
Does the transaction consume something the seller cannot recover: an organ, their health, an irreversible stretch of time?
This is a one-off, unrevisable payment with no chance to correct it afterwards
Add a cooling-off period, volume caps and long-term follow-up — or do not open it
Would allocating by willingness to pay change the standing the thing confers — a vote, an honour, citizenship, a verdict?
Its value rested on being unbuyable, so what is bought is no longer the original
Keep it one-per-person or by qualification, and set no price at all

answer_en.tail: Two closing principles: **first, do not price what runs on 'they were willing anyway'; where the thing runs on 'scarcity must be allocated', a price is often fairer and more transparent than a queue.** Second, if a price is unavoidable, put the exit clause and the after-the-fact protections ahead of it — those two lines shape the outcome more than the figure does.

hooks.text: **不用钱分配，就一定干净吗**：排队奖励有闲的人，按需要分配把认定权变成新的稀缺资源，按资历锁死年轻人，靠人脉分配则把价码压进不透明也无法拒绝的人情里。器官名单、学区、公立医院的加号、稀缺岗位的推荐都是现成例子。那么在一件具体的事情上，该怎么比较各种分配方式的腐蚀程度，而不是笼统地问市场对不对？
hooks.text_en: **Is an allocation without money necessarily clean?** Queues reward those with time to spare; allocation by need turns the power to certify need into the new scarce resource; seniority locks out the young; and allocation through connections buries the price in favours that are neither transparent nor refusable. Organ lists, school catchments, the extra slot at a public hospital, the referral into a scarce job — the examples are everywhere. So for any particular good, how should we compare the corruption of different allocation methods, instead of asking in the abstract whether markets are right?

hooks.text: **「非卖品」的账单去了哪里**：把一样东西移出市场，并不意味着它不再需要钱与人力——只是账单改由税收、捐赠或家人的无偿劳动来付，而最后一项在多数社会里压倒性地落在女性身上。照护、陪伴、临终守候都是如此。那么当我们主张某件事「不该拿钱换」时，是否有义务同时说清楚：谁来付，付多少，以及凭什么由她付？
hooks.text_en: **Where did the bill for the 'unsellable' go?** Taking something off the market does not mean it stops requiring money and labour; it means the bill is now paid by taxation, by donation, or by the unpaid work of family members — and in most societies that last category falls overwhelmingly on women. Care, companionship and sitting with the dying are all of this kind. So when we insist that something must not be exchanged for money, are we obliged to say in the same breath who pays, how much, and on what grounds it should be her?

hooks.text: **有些市场化没有回头路**：挤出效应大多可逆，却不对称——引入报酬容易，撤掉报酬之后，自愿的水平往往回不到原来的高度。这意味着「先用钱试试看」并不是一次可回退的实验。哪些领域一旦标了价就再也退不回去？在真正动手之前，有没有办法先小范围试出这一点？
hooks.text_en: **Some marketisations have no way back**: crowding out is mostly reversible but asymmetric — introducing a payment is easy, yet after it is withdrawn voluntary effort rarely climbs back to where it began. Which means 'let us just try paying for it' is not a reversible experiment. In which domains does a price, once posted, foreclose the return? And is there a way to find that out at small scale before committing?

hooks.text: **当禁令本身成了一种特权**：禁止付费插队、付费快速通道，往往并没有消灭插队，只是把它换了个形式——私立学校、会员制、海外就医、请得起假的人。于是一条禁令实际只对买不起替代品的人生效。这样的禁令，比开放交易更公平，还是更不公平？判断的依据该是什么？
hooks.text_en: **When the prohibition is itself a privilege**: banning paid queue-jumping and paid fast lanes often does not abolish jumping the queue, it only changes its form — private schools, membership schemes, treatment abroad, and those who can afford to take the day off. So the ban binds only those who cannot buy the substitute. Is such a prohibition fairer than an open trade, or less fair? And on what basis should we decide?
